findings.message: Independently recomputed the claimed count increases rather than taking the revision notes at their word: diffing reports/literacy.r7.json against reports/literacy.r8.json confirms blend-words 94->95 (new occurrence of 'steps' in tower-hall's new opening sentence, a side effect the notes also call out), closed-syllable-words 63->64 (new 'mud' x1 in settle-in-the-mud's two edited choice labels), and ing-words 27->29 (new 'climbing' x2 in last-step-up's two edited choice labels). reports/weave-comparison.r8.json shows the same three numbers against the plan and 'ok: true' for all three sets. All three word sets still meet their brief minimum (95/10, 64/8, 29/8) with no conceptMismatches, and reports/literacy.r8.json's perEndingRoute figures (blend-words 11-24, closed-syllable-words 18-27, ing-words 8-12 across all 5 endings) show every set still clears its floor on the shortest route to every one of the 5 endings, including the tightest case, ing-words on home-too-soon, which sits at exactly 8 against a floor of 8 - still a pass, but worth watching if a future revision trims ing content from that route. 'climbing' and 'mud' were independently confirmed to carry their declared patterns correctly in story.r8.json's own text (climb+ing with a free three-letter base; single vowel u between consonants m/d), matching the report's empty conceptMismatches list for both sets.

Diffed story.r7.json against story.r8.json directly (not just read the revision notes): confirmed the only passages that changed are the ten named (watch-the-frog-hop, look-back-at-the-marsh, last-step-up, steady-your-nerves, one-more-breath, settle-in-the-mud, the-stairs, tower-hall, lantern-room, varro) plus the top-level version bump; every other passage, choice target, item/clue effect and ending is byte-identical to r7. I then listed every incoming predecessor of the four shared destinations by script (the-stairs: 9 from 7 passages; tower-hall: 5 from 4; lantern-room: 8 from 6; varro: 6 from 5) and read every one of those predecessor passages' closing text. None of them is contradicted by the new opening sentences: 'the-stairs' ('Whatever Eli had just decided, he turned to climb the stairs.') does not assert whether Eli looked back, so it stays true for 'stone-hop' ('Eli did not look back. They went on to the stairs.'); 'varro' ('However he'd done it, Eli was back on his feet.') is consistent with all four ways a reader arrives there (the three falls ending 'Eli sat up and wiped his eyes', and check-the-book ending '...and stood up'); 'tower-hall' and 'lantern-room' are similarly generic enough to cover all their predecessors, including the ones that never saw the two flagged choices (the-prints/show-lira-the-prints into tower-hall; net-lid/check-on-ash/ladder-climb/help-lira-up into lantern-room). The architecture reasoning in work/revision-notes.r8.md holds up under independent re-checking, and no new continuity error was introduced.

On the substance of the fix: the six edited choice labels do give each fork a small, real point of difference at the moment of choosing (watch-the-frog-hop's 'feeling glad' vs. a quieter 'to yourself'; last-step-up's 'steadily' vs. 'fast, two steps at a time'; steady-your-nerves's 'one careful foot first' vs. 'feeling brave'; one-more-breath's 'hand in hand' vs. 'brave... wave Lira forward'; settle-in-the-mud's 'cool mud' vs. 'brush off the mud, fast'), which is a genuine, if modest, improvement over the prior bare 'A, or B' labels for a reader who is paying attention to voice and pacing rather than just picking an option. Combined with the four destination sentences honestly acknowledging a choice happened without claiming which one, this is a reasonable, honestly-scoped resolution of the 'decorative fork' complaint given the stated constraint (no graph restructuring, no conditional-text engine feature) - better understood as 'each fork now has a small beat' rather than 'each fork now has a distinct consequence', which the revision notes are explicit and correct about.

Two small wording issues in the new destination sentences that a copy pass should catch, neither blocking: (1) 'he'd' in lantern-room ('Whichever way he'd stepped in, Eli was here now.') and in varro ('However he'd done it, Eli was back on his feet.') is the only verb contraction anywhere in this 40-passage story - a full-text scan of story.r8.json finds zero other instances of 've/'d/'ll/'re/'m/n't verb contractions (only possessive 's, as in Eli's, Lira's, the cat's), and the story elsewhere consistently spells out 'he had', 'I am', 'do not', 'cannot'. The two sibling sentences at the-stairs and tower-hall use the full form ('Eli had just decided', 'he had climbed'), so the four parallel sentences are not even consistent with each other. I'd ask for 'he'd' -> 'he had' in both spots for consistency with the book's own established convention, not because 'he'd' is undecodable for this age band. (2) lantern-room now contains two different '-ever' words with two different referents close together: the new opening 'Whichever way he'd stepped in, Eli was here now.' and the pre-existing fourth paragraph 'Whatever was in the Tower's heart was not a villain.' Read back to back these can briefly read as referring to the same uncertainty (how he got in vs. what the crab is); a reader moving quickly could blend the two. Not a factual error, just worth a reword if this passage is touched again.

The four new destination sentences all share one syntactic shape not otherwise used in this story: a fronted subordinate clause with its own subject and verb ('Whatever Eli had just decided,' / 'However he had climbed those last steps,' / 'Whichever way he'd stepped in,' / 'However he'd done it,'), comma, then a main clause. I scanned story.r8.json for this pattern (any sentence opening with When/If/Although/Before/After/Though/Since/While plus a comma) and found exactly one other instance in the whole book, 'Before standing, Eli checked his bag in the mud' (check-the-book) - and that one is a simpler gerund phrase with no embedded subject+verb, unlike the four new sentences. All four stay under the brief's 16-word soft limit (9-13 words each, confirmed by direct count) and reports/validation.r8.json's sentence-length check still reports 0 sentences over 20 words, so this is not a readability-metric failure. But for a book whose average sentence is about 8 words of simple, direct syntax, repeating a genuinely harder-to-parse clause-first structure at all four hubs is worth naming as a mild age-suitability/comprehension-load note for a 10-to-13 dyslexic reader, even though no single sentence is long or indecodable on its own.

Confirmed the explicitly out-of-scope carry-overs are genuinely untouched by this revision and remain present exactly as before, not accidentally fixed or broken: reports/validation.r8.json still reports '3 sentence(s) exceed the brief's 16-word limit', and direct count in story.r8.json confirms the same three 17-word sentences as r7 - late-for-school ('Eli's library book had a map in it, and he was meant to show it in class.'), frog-helped ('She was waiting at the start of the stairs, and she gave him a small, surprised smile.'), home-too-soon ('He looked at his muddy shoes and thought of the marsh, the stairs and the dark hatch.'). reports/literacy.r8.json's perWord counts also confirm 'bus' still occurs exactly once (in 'the-gate', skippable via the 'through-the-gap' opening choice) and 'jumping' is still at 3 occurrences, concentrated in the marsh branch around 'stone-hop' - both unchanged from r7 and still allowed under the set-level ('each set on every route', not every word) rule. None of late-for-school, frog-helped, home-too-soon, the-gate or stone-hop appear in this revision's diff.

Limits of automated detection, restated for this revision: reports/literacy.r8.json and the analyzer behind it detect spelling patterns, not sound - for example the 'Digraph wh' concept list now also includes 'whichever' (new this revision) alongside 'anything'/'nothing' (compounds, not the targeted free-base pattern), and the 'Suffix -ing' concept's 62-token count is a general spelling-pattern count distinct from, and larger than, the specific six-word ing-word-set the brief targets. Syllable counts are estimates from vowel groups, not from how words actually sound, and none of the automated checks judge whether a given child, with their own program's terminology and their own ear, will find 'he'd', 'whichever', 'however' or any other specific word decodable. This review, and the report it checks, remain an AI pre-review, not a substitute for a qualified human structured-literacy reviewer confirming decodability for the child's own program; it is recorded with reviewer.kind 'ai-agent' and is the literacy gate the parent's approval decision depends on, not a replacement for that decision.

Skills practised: reading this story end to end, a child decodes in natural context short words with beginning consonant blends (step, stone, frog, plan, spin, trip, crab, drum), closed-syllable words (cat, map, net, lid, hop, mud, bus) and -ing words (running, jumping, hiding, climbing, glowing, ringing), meeting each set above its stated minimum on every complete route I checked to every one of the 5 endings (blend-words 11-24, closed-syllable-words 18-27, ing-words 8-12, against floors of 10/8/8). Beyond phonics, the child follows cause and effect and sequence across the fall, the marsh, the stairs and the tower, including six round-2 forks that now each carry a small distinguishing beat (a feeling, a pace, a gesture) before rejoining a shared scene; makes inferences from clues (the small wet marks that lead up, the shivering crab, Lira's doubt about the 'hero') that gate some of the later choices; tracks who is speaking across multi-character dialogue; and meets new vocabulary in context with a glossary (lantern, manhole, marsh, hatch, creature, villain, library, promised). The gentle theme of kindness and courage, short average sentence length (about 8 words) and five distinct endings of different emotional weight (triumph x3, bittersweet, setback) suit the stated 10-to-13 age range without talking down to the reader.

shelfSummary.blurb: Eli follows a stray cat down a manhole into a fading magical land and must decide how to help its people, choosing his own path through a marsh, a stairway and a tower toward one of five endings. Along the way he reads and meets, again and again, words with beginning blends, short closed-syllable words and -ing words, in natural sentences rather than a word list.
